title: Introduction to Software Engineering
body:
Introduction to Software Engineering is about everything around writing the code. Every other computer science course hands over a
problem that is already stated and asks for a program. Real work arrives as a person
describing what they want in their own words, and turning that into a specification somebody
can build against is the first task this course teaches.

The second task is keeping a system changeable. A program one person writes in a week is easy
to change because its author remembers all of it. A system a dozen people wrote over four
years is difficult to change because every part reaches into every other part, and a small
edit breaks something far away. That condition is [[Complexity]], the recurring subject of the
course, and [[Coupling and Cohesion]] is how it is measured.

The course also formalises the [[Object Oriented Approach]] that
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] introduced by example and [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]]
uses throughout its [[Java]].

## Topics

### What the discipline covers

[[Fields in software engineering]] places software engineering against [[CS]] and
[[Information Technology]]. Computer science studies what can be computed and at what cost.
Information technology runs and maintains systems that already exist. Software engineering
builds systems to a specification under a budget and a deadline, so it owns the questions the
other two leave alone, such as how long the work will take and what happens when the
requirements change halfway.

[[Project Success]] is measured against schedule, budget and the requirements as stated. A
project can deliver working code and fail all three, which is why the course treats a working
program as a necessary result and not a sufficient one.
[[Projects in software engineering]] covers what a project consists of and [[Metrics]] covers
the attempts to quantify any of it, including lines of code and function points, along with
the ways each measure is gamed once somebody is judged by it.

### The shape of a project

The [[SDLC]], the software development life cycle, names the phases every project passes
through: requirements, design, implementation, testing, maintenance. Maintenance is the
longest of the five in practice and consumes most of the money spent on a system.

The cost of fixing a defect rises steeply with the phase in which it is found. A misunderstood
requirement caught during analysis is a conversation. The same misunderstanding caught after
release means rewriting the code that implements it, the tests that verify it, the
documentation that describes it, and the data already stored in the wrong shape. That
escalation is the economic argument behind every review step in the process.

### Process models

[[Waterfall]] runs the five phases once, in order, finishing each before starting the next. It
assumes the requirements are complete and correct before design begins, and the assumption
holds when the problem is well understood and the specification is fixed by a contract.

[[Agile]] runs the same phases repeatedly over small slices of functionality, delivering
something usable every few weeks and expecting the requirements to move as the customer sees
working software. [[Models]] and [[software development]] cover the range between the two.

The [[YAGNI Principle]], you aren't gonna need it, follows from the second assumption. A
feature nobody has asked for stays unbuilt however likely it looks, because building it costs
time now, adds code to maintain, and is usually wrong about what will actually be needed.
[[Microservices]] is an architectural choice with the same trade shape, splitting a system
into independently deployed services, which lowers the complexity inside each one and raises
it in the network between them.

### Finding out what to build

[[Software Requirements Analysis]] runs in five steps: [[Problem Recognition]], establishing
what the actual problem is, [[Evaluation and Synthesis]] of the possible solutions,
[[Modeling]] of the chosen one, [[Specification]] of what will be built, and [[Review]] with
the people who asked for it. [[System analysis]] covers understanding an existing system
before changing it.

[[Use Case Diagrams]] come late in analysis and describe the system from the outside, as a set
of interactions between an actor and the system:

```
Actor: Student            Actor: Instructor
   |                          |
   +-- Register for course    +-- Post grades
   +-- Drop course            +-- View class list
   +-- View transcript
```

The notation stays deliberately simple because the audience is the customer. Non-technical
stakeholders are the only people who can confirm that the requirements describe what they
actually need, and a diagram they cannot read confirms nothing.

### Two ways to divide a system

[[Design]] has two [[Paradigms]] for decomposing a system, and they cut it along different
axes.

The [[Structured Approach]] divides by function. The program becomes a hierarchy of
procedures, each performing one task, with the data passed between them. Its failure mode is
that the data and the operations on it live apart, so changing the shape of a record means
visiting every procedure that touches it.

The [[Object Oriented Approach]] divides by thing. The program becomes a set of objects, each
holding its own data along with the operations on that data. Changing the shape of a record
means changing one class, because nothing outside it reads the fields directly.

Both aim at the same target, described next.

### Coupling and cohesion

Coupling is how much one module depends on another, and lower is better. Cohesion is how
closely the parts of one module relate to a single purpose, and higher is better. The pair is
the course's measure of whether a design will survive being changed.

```java
// high coupling: Report reaches into Order's fields and knows how a total is computed
class Report {
    double total(Order o) {
        return o.quantity * o.unitPrice * (1 + o.taxRate);
    }
}

// low coupling: Order owns the calculation, Report asks for the answer
class Report {
    double total(Order o) { return o.total(); }
}
```

In the first version, changing how a total is computed, by adding a discount field, means
editing every class that computed one. In the second it means editing `Order`. The difference
is which module knows the rule.

Low cohesion looks like a class named `Utils` holding a date formatter, a database
connection and a string parser, where the only thing the three share is that nobody knew where
else to put them. Nothing groups them, so nobody can predict what belongs there next.

### Object-oriented analysis and design

The pipeline is [[OOA]] to analyse the domain into objects, [[OOD]] to design the classes
those objects become, and [[OOM]] to model the result in a notation others can read.

[[Object Oriented]] programming rests on four ideas. [[Abstraction]] hides detail behind a
name, so a caller uses `account.withdraw(50)` without knowing what is checked inside.
[[Encapsulation]] keeps data together with its operations and restricts outside access, so an
[[Object]] cannot be put into an invalid state from elsewhere. [[Inheritance]] derives one
[[Classes|class]] from another, so shared behaviour is written once. [[Polymorphism]] lets one
call reach different implementations depending on the object's actual type.

```java
Shape[] shapes = { new Circle(3), new Square(4) };
for (Shape s : shapes)
    System.out.println(s.area());   // each call reaches its own class
```

The loop above is written once and works for a shape written next year, because the call is
resolved by the object at run time. That is the mechanism behind extensibility, and the claimed
benefits of the paradigm map onto it directly: extensibility from inheritance and polymorphism,
reliability from [[Unit testing]] against a stable interface, and reusability from a class
carrying its own state.

### Code quality

A [[Code Smells|code smell]] is a surface symptom of a design problem underneath. The code
compiles and passes its tests, and the structure around it is failing. A method three hundred
lines long, the same logic duplicated in four files, and a class that reads another class's
fields directly are all [[Coupling and Cohesion]] failures visible at the level of the text.
The value of naming them is that a symptom is noticeable during review, and the underlying
design problem is not.

[[Exception Handling]] is how a program continues when an operation fails, separating the code
that detects a problem from the code that decides what to do about it. [[Unit testing]] checks
one unit against its specification, and its real function is regression: a change made a year
later is checked against the behaviour that already worked, by somebody who was not there when
it was written.

## Related courses

- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] is where [[Object]], [[Classes]],
  [[Class Relationships]], [[Interface]], [[Implementation]] and [[Function design]] are
  first met by example.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] uses the same [[Java]] object model from the
  implementation side, in [[Inheritance]], [[Polymorphism]] and the [[Abstract Data Type]].
- [[WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS]] applies these principles to a working stack in
  [[MVC]], [[REST APIs]] and [[Microservices]].
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] uses the same error taxonomy, where
  [[Compile Errors]], [[Logic Errors]] and [[Runtime Errors]] match the split in
  [[Assembly Errors]].
- [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] is the largest system in the degree, and
  [[Operating System Structure]] layers it for the [[Complexity]] reasons given here.
- [[PROGRAMMING PARADIGMS]] uses the word [[Paradigms|paradigm]] for the model a
  language is built on, which is a separate axis from the design paradigms here.
- [[HUMAN COMPUTER INTERACTION]] runs this process on the interface, where
  [[Task Analysis]] is requirements gathering by observation and [[Usability Testing]] is
  acceptance testing with the user present.
- [[INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY AND SOCIETY]] asks whether the system should be built,
  which is the question [[Project Success]] leaves out.
